passage:
Leela here, and yes, I’m the person who makes everyone listen to the album. Francis, you asked when it started. I was fourteen and lonely. The songs said things I couldn’t.
Now our fan group chat has a hundred and forty people, and I finally feel understood.
Last month my cousin Neel said the band was overrated, and I nearly cried. I got so angry that I typed a whole paragraph. It felt personal, like he insulted me.
Then I stopped. Neel was just saying his opinion. I deleted the paragraph. But I’m still not sure whether I was wrong to be so defensive. It still stings when someone criticises them.

qa.q: How old was Leela when the fandom started?
qa.a: Leela was fourteen when it started, feeling lonely.

qa.q: Why did Leela feel so upset when Neel called the band overrated?
qa.a: The band had become part of who Leela is, so criticism of the band felt like an insult to Leela personally, and it brought anger and near tears.

qa.q: What choice did Leela make after typing the long paragraph?
qa.a: Leela stopped, remembered that Neel was giving an opinion, and deleted the paragraph instead of sending it.

qa.q: What might Neel have been thinking when he called the band overrated?
qa.a: Neel probably meant it as a casual opinion about music and did not mean to hurt Leela. He may not have known how personal the band felt.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose favourite band is part of identity, feeling understood by fans and defensive at criticism.

passage:
Break time. From the bench I watched Dolma’s group huddle over a phone, whispering lyrics from a series they all loved. Dolma’s face was bright, and she was speaking fast.
Then Arjun walked past. “That show is so cringe, honestly.”
Dolma’s smile dropped. “You haven’t even seen it,” she snapped. Her voice was louder than she probably wanted. Two friends nodded loudly. A third stayed silent.
Arjun shrugged and left. Dolma’s jaw stayed tight for the whole break, though she said, “I don’t even care.”
I’m Shreya, and I can’t know what Dolma was thinking. But I noticed she kept checking the door.

qa.q: What were Dolma and her group doing at break time?
qa.a: They were huddled over a phone, whispering lyrics from a series they all loved.

qa.q: What might Dolma really have felt when she said she did not care?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or defensive. Her tight jaw and the fact that she kept checking the door suggest she cared, though Shreya could not be sure.

qa.q: How could a friend help Dolma after Arjun's comment?
qa.a: A friend could sit quietly with Dolma and remind her that Arjun's opinion was about a show, not about her, and that liking it is fine.

qa.q: How might the silent third friend in the group have felt?
qa.a: The third friend may have felt torn or unsure, agreeing with Dolma but not wanting to join the argument. The passage does not say.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a teenager treat criticism of a series as personal, defending it in front of friends.

passage: Vandana's school bag was covered in Neon Monsoon pins, and her phone wallpaper was the band's latest album cover. In her Pune classroom she was 'the Monsoon girl', and she liked it. Online she had friends in five cities who knew every lyric. So when Rashmi said at lunch, 'Their new song is honestly just noise,' Vandana's face went hot. 'You don't even understand their music,' she snapped, louder than she meant. The table went quiet. Rashmi raised her hands. 'Okay! It's just a song.' It wasn't just a song to Vandana. She spent the afternoon replaying the words, as if Rashmi had insulted her and not a band. That night she messaged Rashmi: 'Sorry I snapped. They just mean a lot to me.'

qa.q: What was on Vandana's phone wallpaper?
qa.a: The band's latest album cover.

qa.q: Why did Vandana snap at Rashmi?
qa.a: She felt hurt and defensive, as if criticism of the band was an attack on her.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped the friendship afterwards?
qa.a: She messaged Rashmi to apologise for snapping and explained that the band means a lot to her.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt when Vandana snapped?
qa.a: Surprised and a little hurt, since she thought she was just sharing an opinion about a song.

grounding: A teenager's favourite band becomes part of who she is, so criticism of it feels personal.

passage:
'Dinner, Ishita!' Rashmi called.
'Two minutes, Mumma, the finale thread is live!'
'What finale?'
'The Glass Crown. The series. The one I've watched four times.' Ishita came to the table in a T-shirt printed with a cracked crown. 'Everyone in the fandom is losing it.'
Her brother Kartik smirked. 'It's a show about sad people in capes.'
Ishita put her fork down. 'Don't. You don't get it.'
'It's just a show—'
'It's not just a show! Those people online are the only ones who understand me!'
The table went quiet. Rashmi reached across and touched her hand. 'Then tell me what it's about. Properly. I want to understand too.'
Ishita blinked, then slowly began explaining the first episode.

qa.q: How many times had Ishita watched the series?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What does Ishita's outburst about 'the only ones who understand me' suggest?
qa.a: She feels deeply attached and defensive, as if mocking the show mocks her, and somewhat lonely outside the fandom.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that calmed things?
qa.a: She touched Ishita's hand and asked her to explain the show properly, showing interest instead of dismissing it.

qa.q: How might Kartik see Ishita's reaction?
qa.a: He probably meant it as teasing and was surprised by how personally she took it.

grounding: A teenager's favourite series has become part of her identity, and teasing about it feels personal.

passage: At fifteen, I was the biggest fan of the Riverfall books in our school. I'd read all seven twice, written fan fiction, and joined an online group of three thousand readers. I signed my notebooks with the heroine's name. So when Naveen said in English class that the books were 'badly written and overrated', I felt as if he'd slapped me. I argued so hard that the teacher had to stop me. Later I realised I'd said more that day than in the whole term. Naveen wasn't insulting me. He was talking about books. But the books were so tied up with who I was that I couldn't tell the difference. I'm Shreya. I still love Riverfall. I just try to remember I'm more than a fan.

qa.q: How many readers were in the online group?
qa.a: Three thousand.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Naveen called the books overrated?
qa.a: Shreya felt as if slapped, hurt and defensive, as though the criticism was personal.

qa.q: What could Shreya do the next time someone criticises a favourite thing?
qa.a: Pause and remember they're talking about the thing, not about Shreya, then share a view calmly.

qa.q: How might Naveen have seen Shreya's reaction in class?
qa.a: He was only giving an opinion about books, so he was likely surprised by how hard Shreya argued.

grounding: A teenager's favourite book series becomes part of who they are, so criticism of it feels like a personal attack.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Simran, Class 10, came to see me after a fight in the canteen. Her bag is covered in pins from a boy band from Seoul; her pencil case, even the margins of her notebooks, carry their lyrics. At lunch her friend Uma called the band's new song "lazy" in front of four others. Simran told me, "It felt like she was saying I'm lazy." She shouted, Uma walked off, and the rest of the table took sides. Simran was close to tears describing the fan group online: "They get me. My class doesn't." I didn't criticise the band. I asked what the music gave her; she talked about a hard year and one song that got her through it. Then we talked about how Uma can dislike a song and still like her. She plans to find Uma after practice. I'll check in with her on Friday.

qa.q: What did Uma call the band's new song?
qa.a: Uma called it "lazy".

qa.q: Why did Uma's remark hurt Simran so much?
qa.a: The band is part of who Simran is, so she felt personally attacked and defensive, as if Uma had called her lazy.

qa.q: What might help Simran when she talks with Uma after practice?
qa.a: Separating the song from herself: explaining that the music got her through a hard year, and that Uma can dislike it and still be her friend.

qa.q: How might Uma see the canteen fight?
qa.a: Uma may have meant it as an ordinary opinion about a song and felt hurt and confused by the shouting.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows a teenager whose fandom is part of her identity, feeling understood by fans and defensive when her band is criticised.
